abstract: The global shortage of fresh water has driven the development of innovative technologies for capturing atmospheric water, with fog harvesting being one of the most promising solutions in arid regions [1]. In this field, functional surface texturing has established itself as an advanced engineering tool capable of altering the microtopography and physicochemical properties of materials to improve their performance [3]. Inspired by natural phenomena such as the structures of the Namibian desert beetle, cactus spines, or spider silk, these techniques facilitate the creation of bio-inspired surfaces that optimise nucleation, coalescence and directional transport of droplets [4]. The integration of these nanometric textures has been demonstrated to increase nucleation sites, whilst also mitigating the effects of water anchoring. This has been shown to result in significant increases in collection efficiency when compared to conventional surfaces. Laser surface texturing (LST) is regarded as one of the most advanced surface treatment techniques in current use. This is due to its ability to significantly improve load capacity, wear resistance, and friction coefficient in mechanical components without significantly affecting material volume. In comparison with traditional coating techniques, LST provides several advantages. These include enhanced accuracy and control over design parameters such as size and shape, significantly reduced processing times, compatibility with a wide range of materials, and a reduced environmental impact. By controlling parameters such as pulse duration, fluence, and scanning speed, it is possible to induce periodic and hierarchical patterns that alter topography and surface energy [5]. In particular, the use of ultrashort pulses has proven to be highly effective in the fabrication of nanoscale and microscale structures with minimal heat-affected zones, thus broadening their applicability in sensitive materials [6]. In this study, the aluminium alloy 6063 was used in its T5 condition. This material was selected due to its extensive use in architectural elements and lightweight structures. Its use is extensive in the field of aluminium carpentry, with applications including lightweight facades, curtain walls, windows, doors, railings and shading systems. It offers a balanced combination of mechanical properties, good dimensional stability, very good corrosion resistance, and high surface quality. Furthermore, its optimal extrusion manufacturing conditions make it a highly cost-effective solution for industrial applications. In this study, laser texturing technology was used to determine its influence on environmental water condensation on an aluminium surface. The tests were conducted under standard environmental conditions, at a dry temperature of 19°C and a relative humidity of 78%. In these conditions, the temperature of the dew point was recorded at 15,1°C and the first condensation nuclei began to appear in the centre of the piece. The tested surface consisted of a 40 mm x 40 mm microtextured square with a hexagonal pattern matrix measuring 1 mm on each side. The piece was engraved using a Lansen LS30F fiber laser. The working parameters used were a power of 15 W and a feed rate of 500 mm/s. The textured piece was positioned at a 90° angle relative to the horizontal plane. The condensed area was evaluated by analysing the surface for localized nucleation patterns using a 100x microscope lens with a global shutter coupled to a digital camera with a processing interface via a Raspberry Pi unit. Fig. 1 shows the condensation microdroplets at the beginning of nucleation. The distribution is in order and consistent with the texture matrix that has been applied to the surface. The generation of microdroplets circumvents the engraved areas, thereby establishing a hydrophilic perimeter that is sustained during their growth. As demonstrated in Figure 2, the time sequence is presented in the form of a graph. As is evident, the geometry employed persists in exerting its influence during the phases of growth and fusion. The textured channel is then employed to establish an anchoring perimeter. Ultimately, the droplet undergoes a collapse because of the fusion of multiple hexagons, thereby initiating a new cycle of active nucleation on the surface. Hexagonal pattern texturing using laser technology has shown a significant influence on the control of condensation nuclei. The stages of formation, growth, fusion, and detachment of microdroplets are clearly influenced by the type of geometry used. This modification adjusts the behaviour of the active surface, creating new opportunities for customising materials to enhance their functionality and performance in the field of ambient water capture. Tests carried out on 6063 T5 aluminium with a hexagonal geometry pattern have achieved well-defined details, without defects or alterations in the material. Given the material's widespread industry use and the increasing accessibility of laser technology, this development option is noteworthy [7]. View of condensate distribution (x5).
